lead: The shell is the program that reads your command line and turns it into action. It is also a programming language: the same words can sit in a file and run as a script. The Bourne shell, sh, is the old portable standard; Bash is its widely used successor with extra features. You meet both in login sessions, build scripts and cron jobs. This chapter separates the two roles, shows how a script starts, and explains how a command is found and how success is reported.
prereq: You need Unit 1 command-line interface and basic commands, and Unit 2 file permissions and chmod.

blocks.text: A shell does two jobs. As a command interpreter, it reads a line such as ls -l, expands variables and quotes, finds the program, and asks the kernel to run it. As a programming language, it runs a file of commands one after another, with variables, tests and loops. Interactive use is typing at a prompt; script use is non-interactive execution from a file. Both go through the same parser.

sh is the Bourne shell. Its path is usually /bin/sh. Bash is the Bourne Again SHell, usually /bin/bash. Bash accepts sh syntax and adds arrays, [[ ]] tests, brace expansion and more. A portable script limits itself to POSIX sh features. The POSIX standard defines the common shell language, so a script written for sh runs on many systems. Some syllabi call this shell basics or shell scripting fundamentals.

items: Interactive shell: prompt, history, job control.
Script shell: no prompt, reads a file, exits with a status.

sections.h3: Running a script and finding commands

blocks.text: The first line of a script is the shebang. It starts with #! and gives an absolute interpreter path, for example #!/bin/sh or #!/bin/bash. The kernel reads it when the file is executed directly with ./greet.sh. The file then needs execute permission. Running sh greet.sh does not use the shebang: you chose sh. Running bash greet.sh chooses Bash.

items: Write the script and put the shebang on line 1.
Make it executable: chmod +x greet.sh or chmod 755 greet.sh. 755 means rwxr-xr-x.
Run it as ./greet.sh. The kernel uses the shebang.
Or bypass the shebang: sh greet.sh or bash greet.sh.

blocks.text: A command name is first checked against shell builtins such as cd, echo and export. If it is not builtin, the shell searches the directories in PATH from left to right. PATH is a colon-separated list such as /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin. The first matching executable file runs. A builtin does not need a file.

After a command finishes, the shell stores its exit status in $?. 0 means success; any non-zero value means failure. if and while use this value, so scripts make decisions from exit status, not from printed text. See conditionals and loops.

Write for sh when a script must run on many machines, including small systems and containers. Use Bash when you need its extras and can require /bin/bash. The shebang should match the features you use. A script with #!/bin/sh but Bash-only syntax may fail when /bin/sh is a smaller shell.

items: Bash arrays: names=(Ravi Asha); echo ${names[1]} prints Asha.
Bash [[ ]]: [[ $name == A* ]] does pattern matching without word splitting.
Bash brace expansion: touch file{1..3}.txt creates three names.
POSIX sh: use [ ], case, for, while and quoted "$var".

blocks.text: Variables and quoting are in shell variables and operators. File redirection is in file input and output. Pipes are in pipes and filters.

figure.caption: Mode 644 refuses direct execution because the execute bit is missing; after chmod 755 the kernel follows #!/bin/sh and the script prints Hi asha. Naming bash or sh skips the shebang, so the interpreter you name runs the file.

spec.title: greet.sh with USER=asha
spec.aria: Running greet.sh directly with mode 644 gives Permission denied; after chmod 755 the kernel reads the shebang and sh prints Hi asha, while naming bash or sh ignores the shebang and also prints Hi asha.

examples.question: A file greet.sh contains two lines. Line 1 is #!/bin/sh. Line 2 is echo "Hi $USER". Assume USER is asha. The file mode is 644. You run ./greet.sh. Then you run chmod 755 greet.sh and run ./greet.sh again. Finally you run bash greet.sh. State each outcome. Explain how bash greet.sh differs from ./greet.sh, and what sh greet.sh would do.
steps: Mode 644 is rw-r--r--. The owner can read and write but cannot execute. ./greet.sh asks the kernel to execute the file, so it fails with Permission denied.
chmod 755 sets rwxr-xr-x. The owner can execute, group and others can read and execute.
./greet.sh now runs. The kernel reads #!/bin/sh and starts /bin/sh on the file. USER is asha, so line 2 prints Hi asha.
bash greet.sh starts Bash explicitly on the file. Bash treats the shebang as a comment and runs the lines. The script uses no Bash-only syntax, so it also prints Hi asha.
sh greet.sh starts sh explicitly; the shebang is again ignored. It prints Hi asha. The shebang matters only for direct execution.
examples.answer: 644 gives Permission denied; 755 lets ./greet.sh print Hi asha; bash greet.sh and sh greet.sh also print Hi asha here because the script is plain sh.

traps: The shebang must be the first line and must use an absolute path. A blank line or a space before #! makes it an ordinary comment.
Running ./script needs execute permission. Running sh script does not; it only needs read permission.
Running sh script ignores the shebang, so the interpreter is sh even if line 1 says bash.
$? is 0 for success. A command that prints an error can still return 0; a command that prints nothing can return 1.
Builtins like cd and echo are not found through PATH. A function or alias can also hide an external program.

quiz.q: What is the shebang and where must it appear?
quiz.a: The shebang is #! followed by an absolute interpreter path, such as #!/bin/sh. It must be the first line of the script.

quiz.q: Why does ./greet.sh fail with mode 644 even though the owner can read the file?
quiz.a: ./greet.sh asks the kernel to execute the file. Mode 644 lacks the execute bit, so the kernel refuses with Permission denied. Reading is not enough.

quiz.q: A script begins #!/bin/sh and uses names=(Ravi Asha). You run bash script.sh and sh script.sh. Which is expected to work and why?
quiz.a: bash script.sh works because Bash supports arrays. A POSIX sh may reject the array syntax because arrays are not in POSIX sh.

quiz.q: A script prints nothing and you see $? = 0. Another prints done and $? = 1. Which succeeded? Explain.
quiz.a: The first succeeded: exit status 0 means success. The second failed: exit status 1 is failure. Printed text is not the exit status.

quiz.q: PATH=/home/asha/bin:/usr/bin:/bin. A file /home/asha/bin/hello is executable and /usr/bin/hello also exists. Which runs for command hello? What if hello is a shell function?
quiz.a: The shell searches PATH left to right, so /home/asha/bin/hello runs. A shell function is checked before PATH, so the function runs instead.

quiz.q: Give two Bash extras not in POSIX sh.
quiz.a: Any two: arrays, [[ ]] tests, brace expansion, process substitution.

quiz.q: A script uses #!/bin/sh but calls [[ $x == a* ]]. It works on one machine and fails on another. Explain.
quiz.a: /bin/sh may be Bash on one machine and a smaller POSIX shell such as dash on another. [[ ]] is a Bash feature. Use #!/bin/bash or rewrite with POSIX [ ].

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, /bin/sh is often dash or busybox ash, so portable scripts avoid Bash-only syntax. ShellCheck is a static checker that flags quoting and portability problems. CI pipelines use sh for setup and bash for richer logic. Containers often ship a minimal shell. Search for POSIX shell specification, dash, busybox ash and ShellCheck.
